title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Post-construction clean
audience: Solo operators and team owners of post-construction cleaning businesses who want handover work from builders, developers and property managers in their service area.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a handover need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. For post-construction cleaning, write down the fit-out sizes you can handle with your crew, the price range you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client has handovers. A builder that finishes several fit-outs a year in your area is worth more to a small business than a single job across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. If you cannot state them, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one. The research found no source on how often builders or developers buy handover cleans, so test that assumption with your own enquiries before you rely on it.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who makes the buying decision, and whether the work falls within the licence and insurance you hold. Builders, developers and property managers doing handover are the likely buyers, but the research did not source this, so add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Write one short profile for each segment, as business.gov.au suggests when identifying a target market (24 September 2024). Keep only business contact details published for business use, and do not buy or harvest contact lists. ACMA's guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (last updated 28 March 2019, an older source). Whether the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business depends on its turnover and other factors, so check the OAIC's guidance. Its coverage is not confirmed in the research file.

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a handover is coming
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely in the near future. For post-construction cleaning, the useful signals are a planning permit that has been issued for a commercial fit-out or a building project, a public notice of works, and a public tender for a building project. Some councils publish planning permit registers with suburb and status fields, such as the City of Casey register, so check your own council's register (DataVic, last updated 5 November 2026). A register shows the stage of an application, not when the work will finish, so you must work out the timing yourself and confirm it with the builder. A building permit dataset can show area-level permit activity by suburb or postcode, which helps you decide where to market, but it is not a list of people to contact (DataVic, last updated 28 August 2026). In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists public tenders for public building work, and each agency publishes an annual plan of what it intends to buy (last updated 7 August 2026). Federally, AusTender lists open tenders and publishes awarded contracts of $10,000 or more (Department of Finance, undated). The Commonwealth Cleaning Services Guidelines were revoked from 1 July 2014, so do not use them as current tender rules (PM&C, 2014).

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: Before you make an offer, confirm the scope, your capacity and the deadline (Business Queensland, last updated 16 November 2022). A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the project or the notice. It makes one specific observation that you can verify from public view or from the builder's own published material, such as a permit or a notice about works. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined handover or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. ACMA says marketing messages need consent, and that consent should be recorded. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading. About 80 per cent of respondents said unsolicited selling seldom gave useful information or offers, and about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026). A specific message that names you is therefore an advantage as well as a compliance step.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. A pattern to test is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. The research does not source this interval, so treat it as a starting point. Where a builder runs a formal quote process, follow its rules rather than your schedule. Stopping is part of the approach. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. Every unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days (ACMA). At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the fit-out size, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the handover work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, such as planning permits and notices of works, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message and do-not-call rules and the licence rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A small post-construction cleaner covers three suburbs. A council planning permit for a commercial fit-out in one suburb shows an application status change, and the builder's business email address is published on the builder's website.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales message to the builder now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should not send a sales email just because the builder's address is published. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page says publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages (last updated 28 March 2019), and the research file warns not to assume a business-to-business exemption. The permit register also shows the application stage, not the completion date, so the owner cannot tell when a handover will come. So the owner first checks whether the builder has agreed to receive messages or has invited contact. If neither applies, the owner waits for an invitation or uses a route the builder has agreed to. For a phone call, the owner checks the Do Not Call Register guide and the calling-hour limits, and treats them as applying until checked. Any message that does go out names the permit, says how the business learned of it, offers one specific item it could handle, and asks one question. The owner does not enter the site without the builder's invitation and follows the site rules.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact, such as a worker's personal number from a site board.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance the state where the work is done requires before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check the rule for each one you work in. Whether handover work is construction work, and which WHS rules then apply, is not settled by the research.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. Marketing messages need consent, which should be recorded, and every unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days (ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam'). Phone calls to business numbers face the calling-hour limits described in the do-not-call guide (2018 copyright notice). The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing, a permit register or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Its coverage of small business is not confirmed in the research file. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen and the stage it showed.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the handover work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, but remember a register shows stage, not completion date. Never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A builder with several fit-outs inside your service area that you already work near
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A council permit register shows a commercial fit-out in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the builder about the project, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each worker on the site using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the job
Go onto the site to look at the work before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must accurately identify the sender and include correct contact details for at least 30 days; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option that is free, works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. The page as read does not name the Spam Act 2003 and does not cover privacy law. Publisher: Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA).
